prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama on Tuesday making him the first head of state to be hosted by the new administration. Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso steps off his Boeing 747 at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland Monday. It was a long trip -- 6,800 miles (11,000 km) -- for a short meeting -- one hour -- and happened as Obama was preparing his first address to a joint session of Congress. Sitting next to Aso in the White House, Obama said: "The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important. "It is for that reason that the prime minister is the first foreign dignitary to visit me in the Oval Office." Obama said the U.S.-Japanese alliance would be crucial in solving international problems including climate change. "We think we have to work together, not only on issues relating to the Pacific Rim, but throughout the world," Obama added. Aso said the global economy was also on the agenda at their meeting. "We are the number 1 and second biggest economies of the world. We will have to work hand in hand. "I think we are the only two nations which are powerful enough to solve those very critical, vital issue," Aso said. Japan's Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said that being the first to visit the Obama White House was an indication of the priority the new president placed on the relationship. Another topic likely to have been on the agenda was Japan's Asian neighbor North Korea, which U.S. intelligence says is preparing to test a long-range missile. Pyongyang has denied the charge, instead saying it is making preparations to launch a satellite. A test-fire by North Korea in 2006 failed 40 seconds after launch. The missile is thought to have an intended range of about 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), which -- if true -- could give it the capability of striking Alaska or Hawaii. Aso's visit to Washington comes, as his approval rating stands at a meager 11 percent, the second lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Yoshiro Mori, a former prime minister, resigned after his rate bottomed out at 9 percent. Last week his finance minister Shoichi Nakagawa announced he will step down after coming under fire for appearing intoxicated at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome. CNN's Chie Kobayashi contributed to this report.

# Aso's Historic Visit: A Diplomatic First Amid Domestic Struggles

Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso made history on his visit to Washington, D.C., becoming the first foreign head of state to meet with President Barack Obama at the White House since his inauguration. The significance of this diplomatic milestone was underscored by the sheer distance Aso traveled—some 6,800 miles—to participate in a meeting that lasted just one hour, highlighting the priority both nations placed on solidifying their relationship early in the new administration.

During the meeting, President Obama took the opportunity to reaffirm the deep significance of the U.S.-Japan alliance, describing it as "extraordinarily important" not only for bilateral relations but also for addressing pressing global challenges. Among the issues Obama specifically cited was climate change, signaling that the partnership between the two nations would play a pivotal role in tackling environmental concerns on the world stage.

For his part, Prime Minister Aso emphasized the economic dimension of the alliance, noting that Japan and the United States—as the world's two largest economies—bore a special responsibility to collaborate closely in addressing the critical economic issues confronting the global community. This message resonated particularly strongly given the backdrop of international financial turmoil that both nations were navigating at the time.

Beyond the public statements on alliance-building and economic cooperation, security concerns also likely featured prominently in the discussions. North Korea's suspected preparations for a long-range missile test—which Pyongyang has characterized as a satellite launch—represented a pressing regional security matter that almost certainly factored into the leaders' private conversations, given its direct implications for both American and Japanese security interests in the region.

Notably, Aso's visit to Washington came at a politically precarious moment for the Japanese leader domestically. His approval rating had plummeted to a mere 11 percent, marking one of the lowest levels of public support ever recorded for a sitting Japanese prime minister. This stark contrast between Aso's diminished standing at home and his prominent diplomatic role abroad added an intriguing subtext to the visit, raising questions about how the international engagement might—or might not—translate into any domestic political benefit for the embattled leader.

# Aso's Brief but Symbolic Journey to Washington

Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso undertook an extraordinary journey of nearly 6,800 miles to Washington, D.C., for what amounted to a remarkably brief one-hour meeting with President Barack Obama. Despite the fleeting nature of the encounter, its significance was not lost on either side of the Pacific. Aso earned the distinction of becoming the first foreign leader to be officially hosted at the White House under the new Obama administration—a gesture widely interpreted as a deliberate signal of the importance Washington continues to place on its alliance with Tokyo.

The meeting, though short in duration, covered substantial ground. At the forefront of discussions was the enduring U.S.-Japan security alliance, a cornerstone of stability in the Asia-Pacific region for decades. The two leaders also addressed the deteriorating global economic situation, as both nations grappled with the fallout from the financial crisis that had gripped markets worldwide. Additionally, growing concerns over North Korea's missile activity featured prominently in the conversation, reflecting shared anxieties about regional security and the potential for renewed provocations from Pyongyang.

For President Obama, the choice to receive Aso first among foreign dignitaries carried symbolic weight far beyond the meeting's brevity. It served as a clear statement to allies and adversaries alike that the new administration intended to prioritize its relationship with Japan, reaffirming a partnership that has long been central to American strategic interests in Asia.

Yet the timing of this diplomatic gesture came against a backdrop of political turbulence back home for Aso. The Japanese prime minister arrived in Washington carrying the burden of an approval rating that had plummeted to just 11 percent—one of the lowest figures ever recorded for a sitting Japanese leader. This stark unpopularity underscored the fragile political position Aso occupied domestically, even as he was being feted with such a high-profile diplomatic honor abroad.

The juxtaposition was striking: while Obama sought to elevate the U.S.-Japan relationship through this symbolic first meeting, Aso himself was navigating a precarious domestic landscape marked by public discontent and uncertainty over his political future. The visit thus represented not only a moment of diplomatic significance but also a poignant illustration of the sometimes complex relationship between international standing and domestic political fortune.

# Aso Becomes First World Leader to Meet Obama at White House

**WASHINGTON** — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso became the first foreign leader to hold formal talks with President Barack Obama at the White House on Tuesday, a symbolic gesture underscoring the importance both nations place on the U.S.-Japan alliance amid a deepening global economic crisis.

The meeting, held in the Oval Office, comes as both leaders grapple with severe economic downturns in their respective countries. Japan's economy, heavily dependent on exports, has been battered by collapsing global demand, while the United States continues to navigate the fallout from the financial crisis that began in 2008.

"The alliance between the United States and Japan is a cornerstone of peace and stability not just in the Asia-Pacific region, but around the world," Obama said following the talks, flanked by Aso in the Rose Garden.

Aso, whose approval ratings have plummeted amid Japan's economic troubles and questions over his leadership, appeared eager to use the visit to bolster his standing at home. "I am confident that under President Obama's leadership, and working together, Japan and the United States can overcome the current economic difficulties," Aso told reporters.

The two leaders discussed coordinated responses to the global financial crisis, with both sides emphasizing the need for stimulus measures and international cooperation ahead of the G20 summit scheduled for later this year in London.

Security issues also featured prominently in the discussions, including the ongoing U.S. military presence in Okinawa, North Korea's nuclear ambitions, and Japan's role in supporting international reconstruction efforts in Afghanistan. Aso reaffirmed Japan's commitment to extending its refueling mission in the Indian Ocean supporting coalition forces.

The choice of Aso as Obama's first official visitor was seen by analysts as a deliberate signal of continuity in U.S. foreign policy priorities, reinforcing Japan's status as America's key ally in Asia even as the new administration signals interest in expanding engagement with China.

However, the visit has not been without political complications. Aso faces mounting pressure at home, with critics questioning his handling of the economy and speculation swirling about his political future ahead of elections that must be held by autumn.

Analysts noted that while the meeting produced no major policy breakthroughs, the symbolism of the visit—and the imagery of the two leaders shaking hands before the White House press corps—may provide a short-term boost for Aso domestically, even as deeper questions about Japan's economic trajectory remain unresolved.

The two leaders are expected to maintain close contact in the coming months as both nations prepare for the G20 summit and continue coordinating responses to the worsening global downturn.

WASHINGTON (Wire Service) — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama at the White House on Tuesday, becoming the first foreign leader to visit the new administration as the two allies sought to project unity on North Korea's missile program even as Aso struggles with plummeting support at home.

The meeting, held in the Oval Office, focused heavily on Pyongyang's stated intention to launch what it calls a satellite but what U.S., Japanese and South Korean officials believe is a long-range ballistic missile test. Aso and Obama pledged close coordination between Washington and Tokyo, with both leaders warning that any launch would violate United Nations Security Council resolutions.

"We are in full agreement that North Korea's actions pose a serious threat to regional stability," Aso told reporters following the roughly 90-minute meeting. "Japan and the United States will work together, and with our partners in the region, to respond firmly."

Obama, for his part, said the two nations remain committed to the six-party talks aimed at denuclearizing the Korean peninsula, while cautioning that provocative actions by Pyongyang would only deepen its isolation.

"The United States and Japan are of one mind on this issue," Obama said. "We will not accept actions that threaten the security of our allies or destabilize the region."

The two leaders also discussed the global financial crisis, with Aso emphasizing Japan's role in supporting international efforts to stabilize markets, and touched on cooperation in Afghanistan, where Tokyo has faced domestic pressure over the extent of its military and financial contributions.

Symbolism aside, Aso's visit comes at a precarious moment for the Japanese leader. Public opinion polls at home show his approval rating hovering in the teens, battered by a sluggish economy, a series of political missteps, and perceptions that his government has been slow to respond to Japan's deepening recession. Some surveys have placed his support as low as 11 percent, among the lowest ever recorded for a sitting Japanese prime minister.

Opposition lawmakers in Tokyo have seized on the numbers, with some openly questioning whether Aso can remain in office long enough to call the general election required by law before September. Analysts say the Washington trip was intended in part to bolster Aso's diplomatic credentials and project an image of statesmanship ahead of that vote.

"This was as much about optics for a domestic audience as it was about substance," said one Tokyo-based political analyst reached by telephone. "Aso needed a strong performance on the world stage, and North Korea gives him a unifying issue to rally around."

Still, officials in both governments cautioned against reading too much into the symbolism of the visit. A senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss the private conversations, said Obama's team viewed the meeting as an opportunity to reaffirm the U.S.-Japan alliance as a "cornerstone" of American policy in Asia, regardless of political turbulence in Tokyo.

Aso is scheduled to return to Japan later this week, where he faces a parliamentary session likely to be dominated by questions over his handling of the economy and speculation about the timing of national elections.

# Aso First Foreign Leader to Meet Obama Amid Domestic, Regional Pressures

**WASHINGTON** — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso is set to become the first foreign head of government to meet with President Barack Obama at the White House, a diplomatic milestone that underscores Washington's desire to reaffirm the U.S.-Japan alliance as a cornerstone of American strategy in Asia — even as Aso arrives politically weakened at home and facing a tense standoff over North Korea's missile ambitions.

## A Beleaguered Leader

Aso, who took office in September 2008, has seen his approval ratings plummet amid Japan's worst economic downturn in decades. Critics have seized on a string of verbal missteps and questions over his handling of stimulus spending, while his long-ruling Liberal Democratic Party faces growing pressure ahead of elections that must be held before September. Some analysts suggest the Washington visit is, in part, an attempt by Aso to burnish his statesman credentials and project strength to skeptical voters back home.

Despite the political turbulence in Tokyo, U.S. officials have signaled they view the visit as an opportunity to demonstrate continuity in the alliance regardless of Japan's domestic churn — and to send a signal to Beijing and Pyongyang that Washington's commitment to its Asian allies remains firm under the new administration.

## North Korea Looms Large

The meeting comes as tensions escalate over North Korea's announced plans to launch what it describes as a satellite — a move the U.S., Japan, and South Korea suspect is cover for a long-range missile test, potentially of the Taepodong-2, capable of reaching parts of the United States.

Japan has been particularly vocal, with officials in Tokyo warning that any launch that threatens Japanese territory could prompt an interception attempt. Aso is expected to press Obama for a unified, tough response through the United Nations Security Council should Pyongyang proceed, while seeking assurances that Washington will consult closely with Tokyo on any diplomatic or military options.

## Broader Alliance Agenda

Beyond North Korea, the two leaders are expected to discuss coordinated economic stimulus efforts amid the global financial crisis, Japan's role in supporting reconstruction efforts in Afghanistan, and broader cooperation on climate and energy policy.

For Obama, the meeting offers an early chance to set the tone for his Asia policy. For Aso, it's a high-stakes opportunity to show Japanese voters he can command respect on the world stage — even as his political future at home remains very much in doubt.

---
*CNN will continue to follow developments as the leaders meet.*
